source_text: Ὅτι τοίνυν εἷς ἐξ ἀρχῆς ὁ τοῦδε τοῦ παντὸς ποιητὴς θεὸς οὑτωσὶ σκέψασθε, ἵν᾿ ἔχητε καὶ τὸν λογισμὸν ἡμῶν τῆς πίστεως. Εἰ δύο ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἢ πλείους ἦσαν θεοί, ἤτοι ἐν ἑνὶ καὶ ταὐτῷ ἦσαν ἢ ἰδίᾳ ἕκαστος αὐτῶν. Ἐν μὲν οὖν ἑνὶ καὶ ταὐτῷ εἶναι οὐκ ἠδύναντο. Οὐ γὰρ εἰ θεοὶ ὅμοιοι, ἀλλ᾿ ὅτι ἀγένητοι οὐχ ὅμοιοι· τὰ μὲν γὰρ γενητὰ ὅμοια τοῖς παραδείγμασι, τὰ δὲ ἀγένητα ἀνόμοια, οὔτε ἀπό τινος οὔτε πρός τινα γενόμενα. Εἰ δέ, ὡς χεὶρ καὶ ὀφθαλμὸς καὶ ποὺς περὶ ἓν σῶμά εἰσιν τὰ μέρη, ἕνα ἐξ αὐτῶν συμπληροῦντες, ὁ θεὸς εἶς; Καίτοι ὁ μὲν Σωκράτης, παρὸ γενητὸς καὶ φθαρτός, συγκείμενος καὶ διαιρούμενος εἰς μέρη· ὁ δὲ θεὸς ἀγένητος καὶ ἀπαθὴς καὶ ἀδιαίρετος, οὐκ ἄρα συνεστὼς ἐκ μερῶν. Εἰ δὲ ἰδίᾳ ἕκαστος αὐτῶν, ὄντος τοῦ τὸν κόσμον πεποιηκότος ἀνωτέρω τῶν γεγονότων καὶ περὶ ἃ ἐποίησέ τε καὶ ἐκόσμησε, ποῦ· ὁ ἕτερος ἢ οἱ λοιποί; Εἰ γὰρ ὁ μὲν κόσμος σφαιρικὸς ἀποτελεσθεὶς οὐρανοῦ κύκλοις ἀποκέκλεισται, ὁ δὲ τοῦ κόσμου ποιητὴς ἀνωτέρω τῶν γεγονότων ἐπέχων αὐτὸν τῇ τούτων προνοίᾳ, τίς ὁ τοῦ ἑτέρου θεοῦ ἢ τῶν λοιπῶν τόπος; Οὔτε γὰρ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἐστίν, ὅτι ἑτέρου ἐστίν· οὔτε περὶ τὸν κόσμον, ὑπὲρ γὰρ τοῦτον ὁ τοῦ κόσμου ποιητὴς θεός. Εἰ δὲ μήτε ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἐστὶ μήτε περὶ τὸν κόσμον (τὸ γὰρ περὶ αὐτὸν πᾶν ὑπὸ τούτου κατέχεται), ποῦ ἐστιν; Ἀνωτέρω τοῦ κόσμου καὶ τοῦ θεοῦ; Ἐν ἑτέρῳ κόσμῳ ἢ περὶ ἕτερον; Ἀλλ᾿ εἰ μέν ἐστιν ἐν ἑτέρῳ ἢ περὶ ἕτερον, οὔτε περὶ ἡμᾶς ἐστιν ἔτι (οὔ τε γὰρ κόσμου κρατεῖ), οὔτε αὐτὸς δυνάμει μέγας ἐστίν (ἐν γὰρ περιωρισμένῳ τόπῳ ἐστίν). Εἰ δὲ οὔτε ἐν ἑτέρῳ κόσμῳ ἐστὶν (πάντα γὰρ ὑπὸ τούτου πεπλήρωται) οὔτε περὶ ἕτερον (πάντα γὰρ ὑπὸ τούτου κατέχεται), καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν, οὐκ ὄντος ἐν ᾧ ἐστιν. Ἢ τί ποιεῖ, ἑτέρου μὲν ὄντος οὗ ἐστιν ὁ κόσμος, αὐτὸς δὲ ἀνωτέρω ὢν τοῦ ποιητοῦ τοῦ κόσμου, οὐκ ὤν δὲ οὔτε ἐν κόσμῳ οὔτε περὶ κόσμον; Ἀλλ᾿ ἔστι τι ἕτερον, ἵνα που στῇ; Ἀλλ᾿ ὑπὲρ αὐτὸν ὁ θεὸς καὶ τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ. Καὶ τίς ἔσται τόπος, τὰ ὑπὲρ τὸν κόσμον τούτου πεπληρωκότος; Ἀλλὰ προνοεῖ; Καὶ μὴν οὐδέν, εἰ μὴ προνοεῖ, πεποίηκεν. Εἰ δὲ μὴ ποιεῖ μήτε προνοεῖ μήτε ἐστὶ τόπος ἕτερος ἐν ᾧ ἐστιν, εἷς οὗτος ἐξ ἀρχῆς καὶ μόνος ὁ ποιητὴς τοῦ κόσμου θεός.
thought_title: The Universe Has One Creator God
pass_a_gloss: That therefore one from the beginning is the creator of this universe, God, consider in this way, so that you may have also our reasoning of the faith. If two from the beginning or more were gods, either they were in one and the same or each of them was separate. They were not able to be in one and the same. For not if they are similar gods, but because they are uncreated they are not similar; for created things are similar to their patterns, but uncreated things are dissimilar, neither from something nor towards something having been made. But if, as a hand and an eye and a foot are parts around one body, completing one of them, is God one? And yet Socrates, being created and perishable, is composed and divided into parts; but God is uncreated and impassive and indivisible, not therefore consisting of parts. But if each of them is separate, with the one who made the world being above the things that have been made and around which he made and adorned, where is the other or the rest? For if the world, having been completed as a sphere, is enclosed by the circles of heaven, and the creator of the world, holding it above the things that have been made by his providence, what is the place of the other god or the rest? For neither is he in the world, because he is of another; nor around the world, for the creator of the world, God, is above this. But if he is neither in the world nor around the world (for all that is around it is held by him), where is he? Above the world and God? In another world or around another? But if he is in another or around another, he is no longer around us (for he does not rule the world), nor is he himself powerful (for he is in a limited place). But if he is not in another world (for all things have been filled by him) nor around another (for all things are held by him), and he does not exist, not being in that in which he is. Or what does he do, with another being that in which the world is, and he himself being above the creator of the world, not being either in the world or around the world? But is there something else, so that he may stand somewhere? But God is above him and the things of God. And what place will there be, with him having filled the things above the world? But does he provide? And indeed, he has not made anything unless he provides. But if he does not make or provide or there is no other place in which he is, this one from the beginning and alone is the creator of the world, God.
pass_b_english: Consider the reasoning of our faith in this way: from the beginning there is one Creator of this universe, and he is God. If two or more gods had existed from the beginning, they would either have been in one and the same place or each would have been separate. They could not have been in one and the same place, not because they would be similar gods, but because they are uncreated, and uncreated things are dissimilar; they have come neither from something nor toward something. Created things resemble their patterns, but uncreated things do not. If they were like a hand, an eye, and a foot that are parts around one body and complete it together, would that make God one? Yet Socrates, though created, perishable, composed, and divisible into parts, is not like God; God is uncreated, impassive, and indivisible, and therefore does not consist of parts.

But if each god were separate, then where is the other god—or the rest—given that the Maker of the world exists above the things that have come to be and exercises providence over all he made and adorned? If the world has been completed as a sphere and is enclosed by the circles of heaven, and the Creator of the world holds it in his providence from above the things that have been made, what place remains for the other god or gods? He cannot be in the world, because the world belongs to another; he cannot be around the world, because the Creator of the world, God, is above it. If he is neither in the world nor around it—since everything around the world is held by the Creator—then where is he? Above the world and above God? In another world or around another? But if he is in another world or around another, he is no longer around us, for he does not rule this world, nor is he himself powerful, since he would be confined to a limited place. If he is not in another world—because all things have been filled by the Creator—nor around another—because all things are held by the Creator—then he does not exist, having no place in which to exist.

What would he do, while another exists in whom the world is, and he himself is above the Maker of the world, yet is neither in the world nor around it? Is there something else so that he may stand somewhere? But God is above him and the things of God. What place will remain, since the Creator has filled all things above the world? Does he provide? Yet he has made nothing unless he provides. If he neither makes nor provides, and there is no other place in which he exists, then this one—from the beginning and alone—is the Creator of the world, God.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex logical structure of Athenagoras' argument regarding the unity of God and the impossibility of multiple uncreated beings. Pass A preserves the clause structure and nuances of the Greek, while Pass B provides a fluent rendering that maintains the theological distinctions (e.g., uncreated vs. created, impassive, indivisible).

The translation accurately reflects the Greek text, preserving the argument structure, theological distinctions, and logical flow. All key terms like 'one', 'uncreated', and 'creator' are consistently translated. The scriptural citations are not present in this passage, so no issues there. The title 'The Universe Has One Creator God' correctly captures the central argument of the text.
